newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. debt vols sag after retail sales.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. debt vols sag after retail sales.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. debt options slumped following release of May retail sales, a weaker than expected report that touched off a torrid rally in the underlying futures, options traders said.
Volatilities finished slightly lower on the day, reflecting diminished market expectations for a Federal Reserve interest rate hike this summer, traders said.
"The market is definitely taking out the tightening in July and maybe August, too. This was a solid rally," a floor broker in Eurodollar options said.
While increased prospects for steady monetary policy buoyed debt futures, the sentiment also removed some of the recent uncertainty from the market, limiting volatility values, they explained.

Treasury bond volatility opened at 7.90 percent in July and 8.50 percent in September, declined immediately after the retail sales number, then drifted back up through the session, said an options broker for a U.S. banking firm.
July settled at 7.85 percent and September at 8.45 percent, slightly above Wednesday's closing levels.
A Wall Street dealer firm accumulated 5,000 July 112-00 calls throughout the day, which helped underpin nearby volatility, floor traders said.

Other large transactions were a trading firm's purchase of 4,000 September 104-00 puts covered against September futures at 111-03, a sale of 3,000 July 110-00 calls, and a separate sale of 2,000 July 111-00 calls.
U.S. retail sales fell 0.1 percent in May, the third straight monthly decline.
September bond futures ended 25/32 higher at 111-12, and December Eurodollars settled up 11-1/2 basis points at 93.93.

Volatility fell in quarterly Eurodollar options, where it was quoted at 8.0 percent in the September 94.00 strike and 10.0 percent in the December 94.00 strike. One investment bank alone sold sold 4,000 of the September 94.00 straddles.

Short-dated mid-curve options saw volatility rise moderately to 15.3 percent in July and 15.0 percent in September. Selling of September 93.00 puts was a feature in the short dates, with two houses selling 2,000 of the options apiece. Mid-curve options expire in 1997 but are priced from 1998 futures.
